title: Strong Weed Myths: Why THC Percentage Isn't Everything
h1: Seven Myths About Strong Weed, and What Actually Matters
metaDescription: Is the highest THC always best? Seven strong weed myths corrected, from THC percentages to edibles and concentrates, plus what to compare on the menu instead.
excerpt: A bigger THC number doesn't always mean a better time. Seven potency myths, set straight, and a short checklist for shopping smarter.
keyTakeaways: THC percentage tells you **how much THC** is in a product, not how it will feel.
Terpenes, dose, method, tolerance and setting all shape the experience.
Edibles can feel strong at small doses, so allow **two hours or more** before another serving.
Weigh THC alongside freshness, aroma and format, not instead of them.
body:
When people talk about strong weed, they usually mean one number: a high THC percentage. THC matters, but how strong a product feels also depends on its terpenes, your dose and tolerance, how you consume it and where you are. Here are seven common high-THC myths, each with a plain correction, plus a checklist for weighing THC properly.

## Why THC percentage became the yardstick for strong weed

THC percentage is one of the most prominent numbers on most cannabis labels, and Michigan requires every package to list its THC and CBD content. That makes it the easiest way to compare products at a glance.

Potency has also climbed. According to NIDA, THC in cannabis seized by law enforcement rose from about 4% in 1995 to about 16% in 2022. Some flower and concentrates sold in dispensaries now top 40%.

With numbers like that on the shelf, sorting the menu from highest to lowest feels natural. But THC percentage tells you how much THC a product contains, not how it will feel to you.

## Myth 1: The highest THC always means the best high

Does higher THC mean a better high? Not necessarily. More THC means more intensity, and NIDA notes that anxiety and panic are more common with large amounts, strong products or little experience.

The right product is the one that matches your plans and your tolerance, and a mid-range option often gives you plenty, with fewer surprises. Our article on [what counts as high THC](/blog/what-is-considered-high-thc/) puts the numbers in context.

## Myth 2: Low THC means weak weed

Low-THC strains can still produce a clear, noticeable effect, especially if you consume only now and then. Lower-potency flower is also easier to pace: you can enjoy the flavor and take another puff if you want one.

Some products pair THC with CBD or other cannabinoids. Those blends aren't automatically stronger or weaker, just different, and the THC number remains your clearest guide to intensity.

## Myth 3: Two flowers with the same THC feel the same

Two flowers can both test at 22% THC and still differ in terpenes, minor cannabinoids and freshness, differences that may change how each one feels.

A 2022 study of terpene data for about 43,000 samples from six states found that products cluster into distinct chemical types, shaped largely by their terpenes. It also found that commercial labels don't consistently track those differences. Same THC, different chemistry.

Freshness counts, too: aroma fades as flower ages, especially when it's stored warm, bright or open to the air. The idea that these compounds work together is called [the entourage effect](/blog/the-entourage-effect/), and research on it is still developing.

## Myth 4: Edibles only work at high doses

Edibles can feel strong at small doses. When you swallow THC, your liver converts part of it into 11-hydroxy-THC. Animal studies suggest this metabolite is at least as active as THC itself. The CDC notes that effects also arrive later and last longer than with smoking.

Michigan caps an adult-use edible serving at 10 mg of THC, and a smaller amount, such as 2.5 or 5 mg, is a sensible start if you're new. The bigger risk is impatience. Because effects are delayed, people sometimes reach for more while the first dose is still building, so give it at least two hours.

## Myth 5: The label percentage tells you how strong it will feel

The label tells you what's in the product, and that's valuable. How strong it feels depends on how much you take, how you take it, your tolerance and your setting.

A 2020 University of Colorado Boulder study shows the gap. Regular users of concentrates at 70% or 90% THC reached blood THC levels more than double those of flower users, yet both groups reported remarkably similar levels of feeling high. The researchers point to tolerance as one likely reason, and they still urged inexperienced users to be extremely cautious with concentrates.

Our guide to [reading a cannabis label](/blog/how-to-read-a-cannabis-label/) shows where to find every number.

## Myth 6: Only seasoned consumers can handle concentrates

Concentrates such as shatter, wax and live resin are far more potent than flower. NIDA notes that dabbing can send a large amount of THC into your body very quickly. That's why it makes sense to build some experience with flower or vapes first.

Still, handling concentrates is less about status than dose control. An adult who takes a very small amount in a comfortable setting is approaching them sensibly, while a seasoned consumer who overdoes it can still have a rough time.

## Myth 7: Anything below top potency is poor value

Value is the experience you get for what you spend, and that's personal. A very potent product may stretch further per gram, but you might enjoy the flavor and control of a mid-range one more.

Price per milligram of THC is one useful lens, but freshness, aroma, format and fit count too. If you're curious about the high end, read about [the highest-THC strains](/blog/highest-thc-strain/). If you'd like to save, ask about current deals and The Society, our free loyalty program.

## So does THC matter? A shopping checklist that weighs it properly

Yes. THC is the main driver of intensity, so it belongs on your checklist. It just shouldn't be the only thing on it.

- **THC level.** Choose a range that fits your experience and tolerance.
- **Terpenes.** Note the aromas of products you've enjoyed and look for them again.
- **Other cannabinoids.** Check CBD, CBG or CBN if they're listed.
- **Freshness.** Check the harvest date on the label and trust your nose.
- **Format.** Inhaled products act within minutes; edibles take far longer.
- **Your plan.** Decide on dose, timing and setting ahead of time, and never drive after using cannabis.
- **A second opinion.** Our budtenders can help you compare products side by side.

For why the same product can hit differently from one day to the next, read [why cannabis can feel stronger](/blog/why-cannabis-can-feel-stronger/). Weighing strain types? Our [indica vs. sativa guide](/blog/indica-vs-sativa/) explains what those labels can and can't tell you.

faq.a: There's no official line. For flower, some people use about 20% THC as a rough threshold, while concentrates often run far higher. Edibles are measured in milligrams instead, and Michigan caps an adult-use serving at 10 mg. Your tolerance counts as much as the number: a modest product can feel potent to an occasional consumer.

Not necessarily. The 30% flower carries more THC per gram, so each puff carries more, but that doesn't make the experience better. Terpenes, freshness and your tolerance shape how it feels. In one University of Colorado Boulder study, people using far stronger concentrates reported feeling about as high as flower users. Choose the product that suits your plans.

faq.q: Why do some low-THC strains feel stronger?
faq.a: A few reasons. If you consume only now and then, your tolerance is lower, so a modest dose goes further. Terpenes and other compounds may shape the experience, though research is still catching up. Your setting matters too: being tired, stressed or somewhere unfamiliar can make any product feel more intense.

faq.q: Do terpenes really change the high?
faq.a: They may, but the science is young. On terpenes vs THC, think of THC as setting the intensity, while terpenes, the aroma compounds behind citrus, pine and earthy notes, may shape the character. Controlled human studies are still limited, so use terpene profiles as a helpful guide rather than a promise, and note what suits you.

review.notes: Independent fact-check: every cited study and agency page was reopened this session; Michigan law checked against facts/law-facts.json (its michigan.gov and courts.michigan.gov sources were verified by the law refuter and not refetched); High Society claims checked against facts/hs-facts.json. Writer's notes: Nothing implies labels are unreliable or that any product is mislabeled; the label is presented as accurate about contents. No product highlights. No claim that CBD smooths the high. Deals and The Society mentioned without terms. Cross-batch sweep 2026-10-24 (orchestrator, after the fact-check workflow): Smith et al. 2022 (PLoS One, PMC9119530, full text re-read through NCBI efetch) analyzed 89,923 samples, but only 42,843 had terpene data; its terpene, chemotype and label findings rest on that subset (the label comparison is "in terms of terpene profile"), so the sample count in this article now names the subset.
